clues.label: A musical characteristic
clues.text: The collection walks through all twenty-four major and minor keys, no exceptions. In every key you get a free piece paired with a strict fugue.

clues.label: Places the composer lived and worked
clues.text: Almost his whole working life happened in a handful of towns in the middle of the German-speaking lands. He never left that language area. Not once.

clues.label: A biographical detail
clues.text: When he wrote this he was Kapellmeister for a young prince at a small court. The chapel there didn't want fancy church music, so he poured that energy into keyboard pieces — a lot of them for students.

clues.label: An anecdote
clues.text: As a young man he walked several hundred kilometres just to hear a famous organist, then stayed months past his leave and got chewed out when he finally came home.

clues.label: An anecdote
clues.text: If you took piano lessons, you played his little two-part inventions. If you know one organ piece on earth, it's his toccata and fugue — the Halloween one. Twenty children. And the four letters of his last name are a tune in German notation: B-flat, A, C, B-natural.

explanation.summary: A small court in Germany, a man who never left the German-speaking world, and a tour of all twenty-four keys: Johann Sebastian Bach, writing at Köthen.

points.text: Prelude plus fugue, one pair in every key — that's the whole idea of Das wohltemperirte Clavier.
A career stuck in central Germany, with zero foreign travel, is unusual for a big Baroque name. That's Bach.
The court is Köthen. Bach worked for Prince Leopold from 1717 to 1723, and Book I is dated 1722. Easy trap: the famous Leipzig years start the next year.
The long walk was to Lübeck, to hear Dieterich Buxtehude.
Inventions, the D-minor toccata, twenty kids, and B-flat–A–C–B-natural. In German notation B-natural is H, so that motif spells BACH.
